newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Italy, Spain face New Year hangover.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Italy, Spain face New Year hangover.

text.p: High-yielding Italian and Spanish bonds, after revelling in a year of sharp outperformance, could suffer a hangover in 1997, analysts said on Monday.

Yield spreads of Bonos and BTPs over German Bunds narrowed significantly last year as the market estimated Spain and Italy had a fighting chance of making the grade for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). But the tone in 1997 could change.
"For the first time in ages we are advising people to sell Spain and Italy," said Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London.
"Convergence optimism has gone too far, and there's little point in holding these markets any longer," Reed said.
Analysts said investors would be increasingly concerned that Italy, in particular, had little chance of bringing its finances into line in time to secure a place at the start of EMU in 1997.
Last week, the Italian Treasury announced that Italy had run up a 1996 public deficit of 138.50 trillion lire -- exceeding the 123 trillion lira government target.
Reed said there was unlikely to be a sharp move back to the high yield spreads seen at the end of 1995, but rather a gradual drift upwards.

At the end of 1995, benchmark 10-year Spanish bonds were yielding 400 basis points more than comparable Bunds and Italian BTPs were at around 500 basis points. The 10-year Bono/Bund spread was at 96 points by 1200 GMT, while the BTP/Bund spread was at 168 points.

Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London, said that the EMU bandwagon would continue to trundle along in the first half of the year, but with a considerable loss of momentum.
"In the second half, EMU cautions will be paramount and there will be a major reassessment," said Shah. "Spain and Italy are the markets with the most to lose."

He said the Spanish spread could tighten further, perhaps as low as 85 basis points, but it would then head out to 125 basis points. The BTP/Bund spread was likely to head to 150 basis points before widening back to 225 points, he said.

Brian Venables, senior bond analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam, said Spain was more likely to meet the Maastrich criteria than Italy, and the 10-year spread could fall below 80 basis points.
But because of investors' tendency to lump Spain and Italy together, analysts said a move out of Italy could spell bad news for Spain too.
"Fund managers will be tempted to lock in profits on Italy as sheer cash and that could cause Spain to suffer in sympathy," Venables said.

He said overseas investors were unlikely to commit new money to the market as they were already overweight in high yeilders. However, there may be some purchasing from domestic buyers who were crowded out in 1996 by the rush of foreign buying.
Shah said international investors will be on the lookout for alternatives.
He said Irish bonds were underestimated, and offered good value, while British gilts were also attractive despite the political threat of a general election before the end of May.
Venables said gilts were a buy at a spread over Bunds of 200, although he was reluctant to be bullish until after the election.

"The natural trade is to switch out of high yielders into Germany, but we're saying "Don't do that,'" said Reed. "We think investors should switch out of Europe, except the UK, and into the dollar bloc."
